chapter_theme: Ten asiriyappa poems to the Lord of Otriyur that argue one thing from ten sides: everything is his form, so nothing can be said of him that is not also its opposite. The cosmos is his body limb by limb; he takes the colour each sect gives him like crystal; his heroic deeds are done on his own limbs; all souls rise in him like waves; his marks and weapons are a picture-language for those who cannot read him; his qualities are a list of paradoxes that bewilder each time they are thought. Against this stands the body, drawn as a sea of humours, foam-white hair and shark-like hunger, which his feet alone carry across; and the poet, who lays father, mother, caste, knowledge, the five senses and all else at those feet and ends in a litany of hail.
structure_note: The work is a single ten-part poem (ஒருபா ஒருபஃது), each part ending on the shrine's name. 954 is the cosmic body; 955 to 957 the one form behind sects, deeds and souls; 958 to 960 the paradoxes; 961 the body as sea and the feet as ship; 962 the poet's surrender; 963 the litany. Each poem closes with a question of the same shape, who on the wide earth can know, say or be accepted, except those who have his grace. The verse keys 954 to 963 are the tool's seq numbers for the ten parts.

954.reading: Lord of great Otriyur, where the earth-maiden wears the warring sea as her girdle: who has gained a form like yours? The lightning is your matted hair, the settled cosmos the shape of your head, fire, sun and cool moon the three lights of your eyes, the stars the garland of your own light, the sky where the gods dwell your body, the eight directions your shoulders, the great sea your garment, the earth-disk your loins, the serpent your feet's custom, the ceaseless wind your breath, all unfailing sound your speech, the flawless knowledge spread through every life your awareness; the standing, shrinking and spreading of the world are your work, making and destroying its effort, and the blinking and opening of your eyes; and in forms of two kinds, three gunas, four births, five senses, six sects, seven worlds and eight shapes, beyond count, in every measure, you join and stand as each thing.
954.nuance: The cosmos is read as the god's body member by member, the reverse of the Siddhar habit of reading the body as cosmos. The count from two to eight (துப்புரு இருவகை, three gunas, four wombs, five senses, six sects, seven worlds, eight murtis) folds the sects (சமயம்) into his body with everything else. மணிமுடிப் பாந்தள் நின் தாளினை வழக்கே (the jewelled-crowned serpent is the custom of your feet) is obscure; the serpent that bears the earth may be meant.

955.reading: 'The one with the woman at his side', 'the one who dances in the dead of night', 'wearer of tiger skin and bone', 'practiser of a life that wanders for alms', 'Mal with Lakshmi and the four-faced one', 'formless and formed', 'he exists', 'he does not', 'untiring', 'one who tires', 'the First', 'the lord of the asoka', 'the ancient one shining under the bodhi': looking at the state of people who quarrel, confused in the plurality of their settled books beyond what they themselves can know, you became for each of them what each took you to be, like crystal taking the colour of what it rests on: that is your form, Lord of Otriyur.
955.nuance: The list runs through Saiva iconography, Vaishnava and Brahma, theism and atheism (உளன், இலன்), and the Jaina and Buddhist teachers (அசோகினன், போதியிற் பொலிந்த புராணன்), and the crystal (பளிங்கு) explains why all are right and none complete. The verse does not rank the sects; it makes their quarrel the colour and him the clear stone.

956.reading: Great one who are the one for the world that has form: since there is nothing here other than your form, whatever thing is here is a limb of yours; so burning the three cities, circling the old earth to end its sorrow, cutting off the sacrifice-god's head, crushing the shoulders of the ruler of the long sky, removing one face of the high Brahmin, burning the flower-arrowed Kama with a glance, pressing the demon with your toe until his strength failed, crushing Death with a look: all such heroic deeds, since they were done where you stand, are your own doing; those who know the substance, who have seen that those who tell them are no other than you, would they set them in praise, unless it be as things that merely happened?
956.nuance: The argument is that if all is his body, his victories over Tripura, Daksha, Indra (or Ravana), Brahma, Kama, Ravana and Yama are blows struck on his own limbs, so they cannot be praised as prowess. The last three lines (நிகழ்ச்சியில் நிகழின் அல்லது புகழ்ச்சியிற் படுப்பரோ) are read as 'they would not put them in praise, except as happenings', but the syntax is open.

957.reading: All the lives that move in bodies with darkness as their companion, from the lotus-born Brahma who rose knowing the substance downward, differ in form, awareness, rank, service, wealth, strength and kind of work, never parting from their deeds; and in their unlike plurality their conduct, like high waves in the settled sea, rose in you and became in you, grew and shrank and shifted and appeared, mingled with you and stood apart from you. First Lord of unaging body, of Otriyur whose ancient fame never ceases: unless those who have gained your grace know it, will others know this bewilderment within you?
957.nuance: The wave is the figure for the soul's relation to the Lord: the same water, risen and fallen, 'in you and yet apart from you' (நின்னிடையெழுந்து, விரவியும் வேறாய்). இருடுணையாக்கை, bodies whose companion is darkness, is the one phrase that names the souls' bondage. மயக்கு, the bewilderment, is said to be in him, not in the souls.

958.reading: Though you are the word that does not confuse, the whirl in which the rest cannot know your state; though the heart is your dwelling, the stealth by which you hide there until it is stained; though you do the deeds that are done in the world, the nearness by which the fruit of those deeds does not touch you; the beauty of becoming a sea in the minds of those who bow to you wanting joy in your company; nearness to those who come in love and distance to those who do not, every day; being of a nature that melts the bones: I have understood that for those who have seen this, your body too is passed beyond, Lord of Otriyur, great ascetic of lasting fame, with the pure moon on your dense red hair.
958.nuance: Each pair sets a quality against its contrary: clear word and confusing whirl, dwelling in the heart and hiding, doing all deeds and untouched by their fruit. The last clause, கண்டவர் தமக்கே உன் உடல் கழிதல் உண்டென உணர்ந்தேன், is read as 'for those who have seen, even your body is left behind', the seer passing beyond the form; it could instead mean that only the seers know your body passes. The verse does not say which.

959.reading: Wearing the pure moon on your hair is a way of settling 'I am the pure path'; riding the white bull that is dharma's form is a way of performing 'I am the Lord'; for those who do not stand saying 'that, she, he', the thing that taught 'I am the common ground'; being called three-eyed is a shorthand that the three fires of sacrifice are gathered in me; holding the deer of the Veda, a way of declaring 'I am its master'; the trident of three leaves on one stalk, a way of saying 'the three are I'; being called the eight-formed one, a way of teaching 'I am the truth in this world'; being called earth, water, fire, wind and the wide sky, the one of unfailing ancient fame, the one with the army of good spirits, a way of making clear in the world. With these colours and forms your greatness is taught, yet to the self-destroying people who do not understand, who whirl in the richness of word and meaning born among them, led by the men of six duties in Otriyur where recitation never stops, you set them to children's games and sit smiling until they come face to face with you.
959.nuance: The iconography is read as a sign-language, each emblem a sentence beginning 'I am'; the eight forms and the five elements are included. The Brahmins (அறுதொழிலாளர், men of six duties) and the scholars of word-meaning are those who, having the signs, do not read them, and the god's answer is not anger but a smile and a wait: சிறுவர் தம் செய்கையிற் படுத்து, setting them to children's play. முகப்படும் அளவே, until they face you, is the end of the game.

960.reading: Though your greatness is beyond measure, you stand shrunk small within my heart and do not leave; though you are body beyond body, the whole earth is called your form; though you are not within reach, you do not fail the distinction those who love you ask for; though by what is said you are no one's companion, you are the master who gathers the good lives; though you are everywhere, you are no refuge to those in whom deceit stays. Beyond that: the birthless birth, the growthless greatness, the renunciationless renunciation, the unlinked link, the unenjoyed enjoyment, the unsubtle subtlety, the undeparting departure, the unapproaching nearness, the undone deed, the unexcelled excellence; hot and cool, exalted and light, red and green, white and black; you make and destroy the many things that are, you remove and gather, you leave and reach: these and the countless other qualities bewilder each time they are thought, Lord of Otriyur girt by the high sea, so that unless those who say this here shrink their standing in words, who on the wide earth knows your nature?
960.nuance: The paradox pairs (பிறவாப் பிறவி and the rest) are the poem's doctrine: every predicate of the Lord cancels itself. The close draws the consequence for speech, சொல்நிலை சுருங்கின் அல்லது, only by shrinking what one stands on in words can he be known. The one ethical line in the list is that he is no refuge to the deceitful (வஞ்சனை தங்கியவர்), which 963 repeats.

961.reading: The unfilled body, grown long on craving and a burden on the earth, with its wind and bile joined as one and the five long winds beating together, grey hair as foam whitening daily, wrinkled skin as swelling waves, gathered blood filling it as water, the covered cough roaring as its sound, burning hunger and anger striking as sharks, the entrails crying like a flock of water-birds, the bones within the flesh, the many diseases whirling in it, the sinews of arms and legs as its channels, fat as its salt flats, the sounding holes as its mouths and the slimy nose as its tide: in this great sea of the body, those who fall into the whirlpool called enjoyment and gain the grace that cries 'ah, ah' for them, go first to your feet that are the ship, bow in order, set the mast of thought upright, fill the sail of melting love, bind it with the rope of swelling restraint, cut the bright rope of crowding kin, twist the peg of fixed oneness, and in the harsh open called the weight of desire, holding to the blaze of the pure light and stirring with the oar of unshrinking awareness, you take them as on a voyage and land them on the long shore where none crowd, Lord of Otriyur girt by the high sea.
961.nuance: The body is the sea and the god's feet the ship, each part of the voyage given a virtue: thought the mast, love the sail, restraint the rope, oneness the peg, awareness the oar. வாதம் and பித்தம் are the medical humours, as the five winds are the pranas, so the anatomy is the physician's. Several items in the sea-list are unsure (மேதகு நிணமே மெய்ச்சாலாக, கால்கையின் நரம்பே கண்டமாக, துப்புரவு as the whirlpool), and the text has two misprints (உருகிய்வார்வப், தூம்ச்சோதிச்).

962.reading: Lord of Otriyur, since the harsh poor words born in me to praise your unfailing qualities are of a nature not to reach you, I am like a child that cries without stopping for a mother who has gone far and does not hear, bound to her by a nature hard to part from, not knowing its own deeds; confused in countless aeons of births, like the blind gaining sight with the mother come before them, a man of deeds who does not know the gate of bowing at your two feet, unless you who tied the knot made in boundless craving joined with swelling pleasure untie it, I do not know even the least part of this; a man of deeds hiding in the thicket of darkness and longing to see the open ground; father and mother, caste, knowledge, our thought, wealth, the way of the path we go, sorrow and renunciation, purity and wisdom, pleasure and fame and many more, taste, light, touch, sound, smell and appearance: all these that shine I have set together at your feet and stand alone; since there is no refuge but your feet, seeking out the place of meeting that the sight of the weary fails to find, you who are hard to reach, do I know, when I look, what I am now to do?
962.nuance: The surrender list is complete: parents, caste (சாதி), learning, wealth, the path of the soul's going, grief and renunciation alike, and the five sense-objects are laid down together (ஒருங்குடன் வைத்து), so that renunciation itself is among the things renounced. The crying child whose mother cannot hear is the poem's figure for prayer that does not reach; the verse says the knot of craving was tied by the god and only he can loosen it.

963.reading: Hail, ankleted one who raged at Death; hail, First, the root of all; hail, Lord of great Otriyur; hail, First who are the whole; hail, nectar sweeter at each approach; hail, Isa without peer; hail, ornament of those who long; hail, honey of unending sweetness; hail, you who forgot the deceitful; hail, you who took poison as nectar; hail, seed of the sea-girt world; hail, you joined with the twisted forest beast; hail, Hara, the ground of the truth seen before and the rightness that dwells in thought; hail, you named woman-and-man for having both heat and coolness as qualities; hail, Siva, the lamp that sets those who reach you in release; hail Mal, hail Vedic one, hail Supreme, hail Brahmin, hail moon, hail fire, hail Indra, hail Lord, hail immortal, hail beautiful one, hail Kumara, hail dancer, hail Substance: unless one says 'hail, hail' to you until the tongue is calloused, who on the wide earth is fit to be accepted?
963.nuance: The litany names him as every god in turn, Mal, Indra, Kumara, the moon and fire, the conclusion of 954 and 955 turned into worship. Two lines explain an epithet by a reason: he is called woman-and-man because he holds heat and coolness, a naturalistic gloss on Ardhanarisvara. நாத்தழும்பிருக்க, till the tongue is calloused, makes the praise itself the only fitness. புரிவுடை வனமா is obscure (the boar, or the forest beast of the bone?).

links.note: Both dress the cosmos on the god: Tirumular makes the sky the linga, the sea its bathing hall, the stars its garland and the directions Nandi's garment; Pattinathar makes the stars the garland, the sea the garment, the directions the shoulders and the earth the loins. Tirumular pictures a linga in worship; Pattinathar a body with breath, speech and eyes.

Tirumular says the Lord himself stands as the directions, the gods, body, life, tattvas, ocean and mountain; Pattinathar says the same thing member by member and adds, as Tirumular does in his last line, that he is also the one who works it, blinking the eyes that make and destroy.

Both make the sects' quarrel a fault of the sects and not a division in the god: Tirumular's six roads lead to one city and the quarrellers bark at a hill; Pattinathar's quarrellers each see their own colour in a crystal that has none. Neither verse ranks the roads.

The same crystal that takes the colour of what lies against it: in the Kural it is the face showing what is strongest in the heart; in Pattinathar it is the god showing each sect its own belief. The figure explains an appearance by its neighbour in both, but the Kural reads a man and Pattinathar excuses a god.

Tirumular's Lord comes as the many souls and, dwelling with them in form, is one with them and not one; Pattinathar's souls rise in him like waves in the sea, in him and yet apart. Both keep the Siddhanta double statement rather than resolve it.

Tirumular calls those who speak of the unspeakable mutes and says the Lord shows himself to thought grown still as water without waves; Pattinathar's list of self-cancelling predicates ends that only those who shrink their standing in words can know him. Both make the limit of speech the condition of knowing.

Two Siddhar boats: for Sivavakkiyar the body is the boat and the open water the end, so act while it lasts; for Pattinathar the body is the sea itself, with hair for foam and hunger for sharks, and the god's feet are the ship. The same figure carries opposite valuations of the body.

Tirumular's boat across the sea of deeds is austerity and virtue, made fruitful by the Lord; Pattinathar's ship across the sea of the body is the Lord's feet, with love as sail and restraint as rope. The sea is deeds in one and the body's own humours in the other.

Both take the body apart by the physician's categories: Arunagirinathar's bellows of bile bound by the three humours and the senses, Pattinathar's wind and bile joined with the five winds beating. Arunagirinathar asks for the end of such birth; Pattinathar makes the voyage across it the god's own act.

Both confess that their words are too poor for the god and that learning did not help: Arunagirinathar has no great poetry and learned tattvas only to argue; Pattinathar's harsh poor words cannot reach him, so he lays knowledge itself at the feet with everything else.

Tirumular says that to take the poison from the salt sea as nectar is the intent of the shining-throated Isa; Pattinathar hails him as the one who took poison as nectar (நஞ்சினை அமிர்தா நயந்தோய்). Both make the swallowing a disposition, not a rescue.

source_issues: 954 ends with the line 'ஒருபா வொருபதெனவுங் கூறுவர்' (they also call it orupa orupahdu), which is an editor's remark on the work's name and not part of the poem; it is printed inside the unit.
961 has misprints: உருகிய்வார்வப் for உருகிய ஆர்வப், and தூம்ச்சோதிச் for தூய சோதிச் or தூமச்சோதிச்.
959 has ருல for றுல twice (நின்ரும், தெருளநின்ருலகினிற்) and வானேறேறுதல் joined; the sense is recoverable.
The VARIANT_NOTES entry on 961 ('[3] ஆலா - ஓர்வகை நீர்ப்பறவை') is a gloss, not a variant.
